claim: CRISPR/Cas9 technology and the ability to culture, cryopreserve, genetically modify, and subsequently transfer chicken primordial germ cells (PGCs) into sterile surrogate host embryos has expedited the analysis of gene function in the chick.
source: The emergence of CRISPR/Cas9 technology and the ability to culture, cryopreserve, genetically modify, and subsequently transfer chicken primordial germ cells (PGCs) into sterile surrogate host embryos has expedited the analysis of gene function in the chick (Figure 1A; Ballantyne et al., 2021a; Ioannidis et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Idoko-Akoh and McGrew, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 1A showing the methodology.

claim: An IL10 knockout (IL10KO) line was created by introducing a premature in-frame stop codon in exon 1 of the IL10 gene in chicken PGCs, 75 bp downstream of the start codon.
source: We first created an IL10 knockout (IL10KO) line by introducing a premature in-frame stop codon in exon 1 of the IL10 gene in chicken PGCs, 75 bp downstream of the start codon (C26>*; Figure 1B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, D, and supplement 1.

claim: An IL10-Enhancer knockout (IL10EnKO) line was created by deleting a 533 bp genomic fragment encompassing a non-coding sequence located approximately 2.3–2.8 kb upstream of the IL10 transcription start site.
source: To generate a potential expression hypomorph, we created an IL10-Enhancer knockout (IL10EnKO) line by deleting a 533 bp genomic fragment encompassing a non-coding sequence located approximately 2.3–2.8 kb upstream of the IL10 transcription start site, in chicken PGCs (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C, and supplement 2.

claim: The targeted enhancer sequence contains a core of 300 bp with conservation around 85% across multiple avian species, containing perfectly conserved motifs for known transcriptional regulators, including AP1, FOXP3, and members of the NFAT/ETS family.
source: This sequence was targeted based upon alignment of sequences from multiple avian species that identified a core of 300 bp with conservation around 85%, containing perfectly conserved motifs for known transcriptional regulators, including AP1, FOXP3, and members of the NFAT/ETS family (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both IL10KO and IL10EnKO lines produced WT, HET, and HOM offspring at a 1:2:1 Mendelian ratio.
source: Both lines produced WT, HET, and HOM offspring at a 1:2:1 Mendelian ratio (see Supplementary file 1 for detailed G2 bird numbers).
evidence: Supported by breeding data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: IL10 protein was completely absent in LPS-stimulated BMDMs derived from IL10KO HOM embryos.
source: Figure 2A confirms the release of IL10 by LPS-stimulated BMDMs derived from WT embryos and the complete absence of detectable IL10 release by BMDMs derived from IL10KO HOM embryos.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The absence of IL10 in IL10KO HOM BMDMs was associated with a significant increase in nitric oxide production.
source: The absence of IL10 was associated with a significant increase in nitric oxide production that was not additive with the impact of added anti-IL10 antibody (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by Griess assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IL10 expression was reduced by up to 50% in BMDMs derived from IL10KO HET embryos.
source: However, we found that expression of IL10 was reduced by up to 50% in BMDMs derived from IL10KO HET embryos, with a corresponding partial impact on nitric oxide production (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA and Griess assay data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The IL10KO mutation does not exhibit dosage compensation in heterozygotes.
source: However, we found that expression of IL10 was reduced by up to 50% in BMDMs derived from IL10KO HET embryos, with a corresponding partial impact on nitric oxide production (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heterozygotes show approximately 50% reduction in IL10 expression rather than maintaining normal levels through compensation.

claim: IL10KO and IL10EnKO chicken lines were created and raised under SPF conditions in the NARF SPF avian facility.
source: The IL10KO and IL10EnKO chicken lines were created and raised under SPF conditions in the NARF SPF avian facility.
evidence: Direct statement about the housing conditions of the experimental animals.

claim: Close monitoring of IL10KO and IL10EnKO WT, HET, and HOM birds over several months in the SPF environment did not reveal any health issues or adverse phenotypes.
source: Close monitoring of the WT, HET, and HOM birds over several months in that environment did not reveal any health issues or adverse phenotypes.
evidence: Based on observational monitoring data over several months.

claim: The IL10KO and IL10EnKO edits did not significantly affect the post-hatch growth of HET and HOM birds compared to their respective WT controls.
source: The IL10KO and IL10EnKO edits did not significantly affect the post-hatch growth of HET and HOM birds compared to their respective WT controls (Figure 3A and B), although IL10EnKO HET and HOM hens were overall heavier than IL10EnKO WT controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Regular gross post-mortem examination and histopathological analyses revealed no evidence of intestinal pathology in IL10KO HOM and IL10EnKO HOM birds compared to WT controls.
source: Regular gross post-mortem examination of tissues and histopathological analyses of the gastrointestinal tract over several months, using a semiquantitative scoring system (McCafferty et al., 2000), revealed no evidence of intestinal pathology in IL10KO HOM and IL10EnKO HOM birds compared to WT controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by histopathological scoring data shown in Figure 3C and citation to the scoring method.

claim: IL10-deficient chickens do not develop spontaneous colitis, in contrast to IL10-deficient mice.
source: These results are in contrast with the early onset colitis and failure to thrive phenotypes observed in IL10-deficient mouse models in both conventional and SPF environments (Kühn et al., 1993; Redhu et al., 2017; Papoutsopoulou et al., 2021; Büchler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited mouse studies and the absence of pathology in chicken data.

claim: The caecal microbiome of IL10KO WT and HOM birds at 4 weeks of age was dominated by the phylum Firmicutes.
source: The caecal microbiome of both genotypes was dominated by the phylum Firmicutes (Figure 4A) and the most abundant genera were Lactobacillus and Faecalibacterium (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by 16S rDNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The most abundant genera in the caecal microbiome of IL10KO WT and HOM birds were Lactobacillus and Faecalibacterium.
source: The caecal microbiome of both genotypes was dominated by the phylum Firmicutes (Figure 4A) and the most abundant genera were Lactobacillus and Faecalibacterium (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by 16S rDNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LEfSe analysis showed enrichment of the phylum Firmicutes and the genera Defluviitaleaceae_UCG-011 and Paludicola in the IL10KO HOM group.
source: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) analysis showed enrichment of the phylum Firmicutes and the genera Defluviitaleaceae_UCG-011 and Paludicola in the IL10KO HOM group, while the phylum Bacteroidota and the genera Alistipes and UCG_008 were enriched in the WT group (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by LEfSe analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The phylum Bacteroidota and the genera Alistipes and UCG_008 were enriched in the IL10KO WT group compared to HOM.
source: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) effect size (LEfSe) analysis showed enrichment of the phylum Firmicutes and the genera Defluviitaleaceae_UCG-011 and Paludicola in the IL10KO HOM group, while the phylum Bacteroidota and the genera Alistipes and UCG_008 were enriched in the WT group (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by LEfSe analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Principal component analyses showed clear separation of the microbial communities between IL10KO WT and HOM birds based on beta diversity.
source: Principal component analyses showed clear separation of the microbial communities based on beta diversity (Figure 4D; R²=0.25, p=0.017).
evidence: Supported by PCA data shown in Figure 4D with statistical significance.

claim: Mucosal IL10 regulates the composition of the chicken microbiome.
source: These findings confirm that mucosal IL10 regulates the composition of the chicken microbiome.
evidence: Inferred from the observed differences in microbiome composition between IL10KO WT and HOM birds.

claim: IL10KO HOM birds remained healthy when raised in the NARF conventional avian facility.
source: IL10KO HOM birds remained healthy in that environment as they aged.
evidence: Based on observational monitoring data in the conventional facility.

claim: Post-growth hatch rates were comparable between IL10KO WT and HOM hens in the conventional facility, with the exception of a marginal effect on growth that resolved with age.
source: Post-growth hatch rates were comparable between IL10KO WT and HOM hens, with the exception of a marginal effect on growth that resolved with age (Figure 3D); there was also no evidence of overt intestinal pathology in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cellular infiltration scores were significantly higher in the duodenum and proximal colon of both IL10KO WT and HOM birds raised in the conventional facility compared to the SPF environment.
source: Cellular infiltration scores were, however, significantly higher in the duodenum and proximal colon of both IL10KO WT and HOM birds raised in the conventional facility as opposed to the SPF environment (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by histopathological scoring data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Antibody titres to AEV and IBDV were significantly lower in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls.
source: Antibody titres to AEV and IBDV were significantly lower in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls, whereas those to EDS and IBV were significantly higher in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Antibody titres to EDS and IBV were significantly higher in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls.
source: Antibody titres to AEV and IBDV were significantly lower in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls, whereas those to EDS and IBV were significantly higher in IL10KO HOM birds compared to WT controls (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Antibody titres to CAV, ILTV, and NDV were not significantly different between IL10KO HOM birds and WT controls.
source: Antibody titres to CAV, ILTV, and NDV were not significantly different between IL10KO HOM birds and WT controls (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Colonisation of the caeca by C. jejuni in IL10KO HOM birds was significantly lower at 1 week post-infection in the first cohort, with a median of 4.8 log10 CFU g–1 compared to >9 log10 CFU g–1 in WT birds.
source: In the first cohort, colonisation of the caeca by C. jejuni in IL10KO HOM birds was significantly lower at 1 week post-infection, with a median of 4.8 log10 CFU g–1 compared to >9 log10 CFU g–1 in WT birds (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial colonisation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: By 2 weeks post-infection with C. jejuni in the first cohort, all groups had caecal colonisation at >9 log10 CFU g–1.
source: However, this was not sustained and by 2 weeks post-infection, all groups had caecal colonisation at >9 log10 CFU g–1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial colonisation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the second C. jejuni cohort, caecal colonisation decreased by ~2 log10 CFU g–1 in IL10KO HOM birds at 2 weeks post-infection relative to WT birds.
source: In the second cohort, median counts were not statistically different between IL10KO WT and HOM birds at 1 week post-infection, but caecal colonisation decreased by ~2 log10 CFU g–1 in IL10KO HOM birds at 2 weeks post-infection relative to WT birds (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by bacterial colonisation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The caecal mucosa of IL10KO HOM birds infected with C. jejuni presents with significantly increased numbers of lymphocytes and plasma cells, admixed with infiltrating heterophils, when compared to WT and IL10KO HET birds in both cohorts.
source: Histopathological analysis revealed that the caecal mucosa of IL10KO HOM birds presents with significantly increased numbers of lymphocytes and plasma cells, admixed with infiltrating heterophils, when compared to WT and IL10KO HET birds in both cohorts (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Large increases in expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and other effectors, notably Nos2, were detected in the IL10KO HOM caecum relative to WT following C. jejuni infection in both cohorts.
source: In both cohorts, we detected large increases in expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and other effectors, notably Nos2, in the IL10KO HOM caecum relative to WT (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by multiplex qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The impact of lack of IL10 on S. Typhimurium bacterial burden in caecum, liver, and spleen was marginal at 1 week post-infection.
source: The impact of lack of IL10 on bacterial burden in caecum, liver, and spleen was marginal at 1 week, but by 2 weeks the majority of IL10KO HOM birds had eliminated the pathogen, whereas WT birds retained bacteria in both caecum and spleen (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: By 2 weeks post-infection with S. Typhimurium, the majority of IL10KO HOM birds had eliminated the pathogen, whereas WT birds retained bacteria in both caecum and spleen.
source: The impact of lack of IL10 on bacterial burden in caecum, liver, and spleen was marginal at 1 week, but by 2 weeks the majority of IL10KO HOM birds had eliminated the pathogen, whereas WT birds retained bacteria in both caecum and spleen (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Enhanced lymphoplasmacytic and heterophil infiltration was observed in the ileum and caecum of IL10KO HOM compared to WT or IL10KO HET birds at both intervals after S. Typhimurium infection.
source: Enhanced lymphoplasmacytic and heterophil infiltration was observed in the ileum and caecum of IL10KO HOM compared to WT or IL10KO HET birds at both intervals after S. Typhimurium infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Analysis of inflammatory gene expression by multiplex qRT-PCR revealed a substantial increase in response in the IL10KO HOM birds relative to WT following S. Typhimurium infection.
source: As observed following the C. jejuni challenge, analysis of inflammatory gene expression by multiplex qRT-PCR revealed a substantial increase in response in the IL10KO HOM birds relative to WT (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by multiplex qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The absence of IL10 leads to a sustained increase in inflammation in response to enteric bacterial infection that is also associated with more effective clearance.
source: In summary, the absence of IL10 leads to a sustained increase in inflammation in response to enteric bacterial infection that is also associated with more effective clearance.
evidence: Summary statement based on the combined bacterial infection data.

claim: Eimeria infection of chickens induces a robust IFNγ-driven immune response with evidence of higher IL10 expression associated with increased susceptibility.
source: Eimeria infection of chickens induces a robust IFNγ-driven immune response with evidence of higher IL10 expression associated with increased susceptibility (Rothwell et al., 2004; Bremner et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Average parasite replication was almost ablated in IL10KO HOM and significantly reduced in IL10EnKO HOM chickens compared to their respective WT controls following E. tenella infection.
source: Parasite burden was almost ablated in IL10KO HOM and significantly reduced in IL10EnKO HOM chickens compared to their respective WT controls, whereas HET mutations had no significant effect in either case (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: HET mutations in IL10KO and IL10EnKO had no significant effect on E. tenella parasite burden.
source: Parasite burden was almost ablated in IL10KO HOM and significantly reduced in IL10EnKO HOM chickens compared to their respective WT controls, whereas HET mutations had no significant effect in either case (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Histology confirmed reduced parasite replication in IL10KO HOM chickens, with dense populations of late-stage gametocytes observed in WT caecal tissues and correspondingly very sparse numbers in IL10KO HOM chickens.
source: Histology confirmed reduced parasite replication in IL10KO HOM chickens, with dense populations of late-stage gametocytes observed in WT caecal tissues and correspondingly very sparse numbers in IL10KO HOM chickens (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Supported by histological images shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The selective reduction of parasite burden in IL10KO HOM chickens infected with E. tenella was associated with a significant increase in caecal lesion score and a substantial reduction in body weight gain over the 6-day challenge interval.
source: This selective reduction of parasite burden in IL10KO HOM chickens was associated with a significant increase in caecal lesion score and a substantial reduction in body weight gain over the 6-day challenge interval (Figure 7E and G).
evidence: Supported by lesion score and body weight data shown in Figure 7E and G.

claim: Both IL10KO HET and IL10EnKO HOM and HET showed reduced caecal lesion scores and had no effect on body weight gain compared to their respective WT controls following E. tenella infection.
source: By contrast, both IL10KO HET and IL10EnKO HOM and HET (each anticipated to reduce IL10 expression) showed reduced caecal lesion scores and had no effect on body weight gain compared to their respective WT controls (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Supported by lesion score and body weight data shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: The greatly reduced E. tenella replication in IL10KO HOM was reflected in corresponding reduced excretion of oocysts.
source: Figure 8A confirms the greatly reduced E. tenella replication in IL10KO HOM, which was reflected in corresponding reduced excretion of oocysts (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and oocyst count data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Lesions associated with E. tenella infection were accelerated in IL10KO HOM chickens compared to WT.
source: Lesions associated with E. tenella infection were accelerated in IL10KO HOM chickens compared to WT (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by lesion score data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The adverse impact of IL10KO HOM on body weight gain following E. tenella infection was sustained to day 8 and showed signs of recovery by day 10.
source: The adverse impact of IL10KO HOM on body weight gain was sustained to day 8 and showed signs of recovery by day 10 (Figure 8D), likely due to complete pathogen elimination (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by body weight gain data shown in Figure 8D and parasite burden data in Figure 8A.

claim: Inflammatory gene expression was elevated in the caecum of IL10KO HOM birds prior to E. tenella challenge (day 0).
source: Consistent with the mild inflammatory cell infiltration in IL10KO HOM birds noted in Figure 7D, inflammatory gene expression was elevated in the caecum prior to challenge (day 0).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The greatest difference in inflammatory gene expression in IL10KO HOM birds relative to WT following E. tenella infection was detected on day 6, during the period of peak pathology.
source: The greatest difference in IL10KO HOM birds relative to WT was detected on day 6, during the period of peak pathology (Figure 8C and E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and lesion score data shown in Figure 8C and E.

claim: IL10-deficient chickens did not exhibit spontaneous colitis, unlike IL10-deficient mice and humans.
source: In vitro analysis of macrophage response to lipopolysaccharide confirmed the loss of IL10 protein expression, the lack of dosage compensation in heterozygotes, and prevention of autocrine inhibition of nitric oxide production in homozygous IL10 knockout macrophages. IL10-deficiency significantly altered the composition of the caecal microbiome, but unlike IL10-deficient mice and humans, IL10-deficient chickens did not exhibit spontaneous colitis.
evidence: Supported by the absence of spontaneous colitis in histopathological analyses and comparison with cited mouse and human studies.

claim: Following experimental challenge with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium or Campylobacter jejuni in IL10-deficient chickens, enhanced clearance of the pathogens was associated with elevated transcription of pro-inflammatory genes and increased infiltration of inflammatory cells into gut mucosa.
source: Following experimental challenge with Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium or Campylobacter jejuni in IL10-deficient chickens, enhanced clearance of the pathogens was associated with elevated transcription of pro-inflammatory genes and increased infiltration of inflammatory cells into gut mucosa.
evidence: Supported by bacterial burden, gene expression, and histopathological data from the bacterial challenge experiments.

claim: In IL10-deficient chickens challenged with the parasite Eimeria tenella, pathogen clearance was accelerated but caecal lesions were more severe and weight gain was compromised.
source: In IL10-deficient chickens challenged with the parasite Eimeria tenella, pathogen clearance was accelerated but caecal lesions were more severe and weight gain was compromised.
evidence: Supported by parasite burden, lesion score, and body weight gain data from the Eimeria challenge experiments.

claim: Neither the heterozygous IL10 knockout nor a homozygous IL10 enhancer mutation had a major effect on pathogen clearance or inflammation in any of the challenge models.
source: Neither the heterozygous IL10 knockout nor a homozygous IL10 enhancer mutation had a major effect on pathogen clearance or inflammation in any of the challenge models.
evidence: Supported by the combined data from all challenge experiments showing minimal effects of HET and IL10EnKO HOM mutations.

claim: The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL10 has long been recognised as an essential feedback regulator of intestinal inflammation in mammals.
source: The anti-inflammatory cytokine, interleukin 10 (IL10), has long been recognised as an essential feedback regulator of intestinal inflammation in mammals (reviewed in Saraiva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: IL10-deficient mice generated by homologous recombination developed spontaneous enterocolitis.
source: IL10-deficient mice generated by homologous recombination developed spontaneous enterocolitis (Kühn et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original study.

claim: Components of the intestinal microbiome were essential to the development of pathology in IL10-deficient mice and determined the extent and location of lesions.
source: Subsequent studies revealed that components of the intestinal microbiome were essential to the development of pathology and determined the extent and location of lesions (Sellon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to a subsequent study.

claim: In humans, homozygous mutations in genes encoding IL10 or its receptor, IL10RA, have been associated with early-onset inflammatory bowel disease.
source: In humans, homozygous mutations in genes encoding IL10 or its receptor, IL10RA, have been associated with early-onset inflammatory bowel disease (Saraiva et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review article.

claim: In mammals, IL10 is produced by both myeloid and T and B lymphoid cells following activation by immune stimuli.
source: In mammals, IL10 is produced by both myeloid and T and B lymphoid cells following activation by immune stimuli (Saraiva et al., 2020; Couper et al., 2008), with subtle differences between mice and humans (Rasquinha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In the specific context of the intestine, conditional deletion of the IL10 and IL10RA genes in mice indicated that production of the ligand by macrophages was not required for pathology, consistent with T cells being the major source of intestinal IL10.
source: In the specific context of the intestine, conditional deletion of the IL10 and IL10RA genes in mice indicated that production of the ligand by macrophages was not required for pathology, consistent with T cells being the major source of intestinal IL10 (Brockmann et al., 2018; Pils et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using conditional deletion.

claim: Macrophage-specific deletion of the IL10RA gene encoding the IL10 receptor was sufficient to elicit spontaneous colitis in mice.
source: By contrast, macrophage-specific deletion of the IL10RA gene encoding the IL10 receptor was sufficient to elicit spontaneous colitis in mice (Bernshtein et al., 2019; Redhu et al., 2017; Zigmond et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies using macrophage-specific deletion.

claim: Both IL10 ligand and receptor are conserved in vertebrates.
source: Both ligand and receptor are conserved in vertebrates, and zebrafish has been discussed as a model for understanding IL10 biology (Piazzon et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation and general knowledge of vertebrate biology.

claim: Chicken IL10 mRNA contains multiple copies of the AUUUA instability motif in the 3'-untranslated region.
source: Like the mammalian transcript, chicken IL10 mRNA contains multiple copies of the AUUUA instability motif in the 3'-untranslated region.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison with mammalian transcripts.

claim: Quantitative variation in IL10 production may contribute to inter-individual or inter-breed variation in infectious disease susceptibility in chickens.
source: We and others have provided evidence that quantitative variation in IL10 production may contribute to inter-individual or inter-breed variation in infectious disease susceptibility in chickens (Russell et al., 2021; Boulton et al., 2018a; Swaggerty et al., 2015; Calenge et al., 2009; Ghebremicael et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The difference in spontaneous colitis phenotype between IL10-deficient chickens and mice may lie in the nature of the chicken intestinal microbiome.
source: Since spontaneous colitis in mice depends upon resident enteric bacteria (Sellon et al., 1998), it is possible that the difference compared to the rodent models lies in the nature of the chicken intestinal microbiome (Bajagai et al., 2024), in which case the changes that we observed in the microbiome of IL10KO HOM chicks may serve to mitigate potential spontaneous intestinal pathology.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on cited mouse studies and observed microbiome differences.

claim: Deletion of IL10 from the genome or selection in favour of low IL10 expression alleles need not necessarily affect production traits in chickens.
source: In any case, the results indicate that deletion of IL10 from the genome or selection in favour of low IL10 expression alleles (Boulton et al., 2018a; Ghebremicael et al., 2008; Boulton et al., 2018b; Freem et al., 2019) need not necessarily affect production traits.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of major growth or health effects in IL10-deficient chickens.

claim: Findings with Campylobacter in IL10KO HOM birds are consistent with elevated intestinal inflammation in a broiler breed with relatively low IL10 expression.
source: Findings with Campylobacter in IL10KO HOM birds are consistent with elevated intestinal inflammation in a broiler breed with relatively low IL10 expression, albeit a significant reduction in caecal colonisation relative to breeds with higher IL10 expression was not observed (Humphrey et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited study on broiler breeds.

claim: Variation in C. jejuni colonisation between timepoints, birds and repeated experiments is typical and has been reported when evaluating vaccines against C. jejuni colonisation.
source: This is typical of C. jejuni colonisation in chickens, where bacterial population structures have been reported to be variable and unpredictable (Coward et al., 2008). Similar variation between time intervals, birds and repeated experiments has been reported when evaluating vaccines against C. jejuni colonisation (e.g. Buckley et al., 2010; Nothaft et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting variability in C. jejuni colonisation.

claim: In mammals, Salmonella has been reported to gain a competitive advantage from intestinal inflammation, both owing to availability of tetrathionate that Salmonella can uniquely use as a respiratory electron acceptor and remodelling of the indigenous microbiota.
source: In mammals, Salmonella has been reported to gain a competitive advantage from intestinal inflammation, both owing to availability of tetrathionate that Salmonella can uniquely use as a respiratory electron acceptor (Winter et al., 2010) and remodelling of the indigenous microbiota (Rogers, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Salmonella pathogenesis in mammals.

claim: It is unclear if Salmonella derives the same benefits during colonisation of the avian intestine as it does in mammals.
source: It is unclear if Salmonella derives the same benefits during colonisation of the avian intestine and the counts of viable bacteria recovered from the caeca of WT and IL10KO HOM birds can only be interpreted as the balance of bacterial growth and killing.
evidence: Speculative statement about the applicability of mammalian findings to avian systems.

claim: Coccidiosis has been estimated to exert costs in excess of £10 billion every year to the chicken production industry.
source: Coccidiosis has been estimated to exert costs in excess of £10 billion every year to the chicken production industry (Blake et al., 2020), with E. tenella among the most common and pathogenic species (Clark et al., 2016; Long et al., 1976).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on the economic impact of coccidiosis.

claim: Feeding antibody to IL10 receptor 2 (but not receptor 1) reduced lost BWG, but had no effect on oocyst shedding.
source: Similarly, feeding antibody to IL10 receptor 2 (but not receptor 1) reduced lost BWG, but had no effect on oocyst shedding (Arendt et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study using anti-IL10 receptor antibodies.

claim: Feeding chickens genetically modified corn expressing IL10 improved BWG and reduced oocyst shedding and caecal lesions.
source: Feeding chickens genetically modified corn (Zea mays) expressing IL10 improved BWG and reduced oocyst shedding and caecal lesions (Lessard et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study using IL10-expressing corn.

claim: The results from feeding studies with IL10-related interventions are consistent with the phenotypes associated with a reduction, rather than complete absence, of IL10 observed in the current study.
source: These results are consistent with the phenotypes associated with a reduction, rather than complete absence, of IL10 observed here.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cited feeding studies with the current experimental results.

claim: IL10KO HOM birds or hypomorphs might be hyper-sensitive to more virulent bacterial infections and viral pathogens, such as avian influenza, that can elicit a cytokine storm.
source: Given the excessive inflammatory activation we observed in non-lethal infections, and the literature in mice, IL10KO HOM birds or hypomorphs might be hyper-sensitive to more virulent bacterial infections and viral pathogens, such as avian influenza, that can elicit a cytokine storm.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on observed inflammatory responses and mouse literature.

claim: IL10KO HOM birds might be primed for a more rapid and effective response to more virulent infections.
source: On the other hand, they may be primed for a more rapid and effective response.
evidence: Speculative alternative prediction based on observed enhanced pathogen clearance.

claim: The findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response.
source: Our findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response and have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
evidence: Summary statement based on the overall experimental findings showing trade-offs between pathogen clearance and pathology.

claim: The findings have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
source: Our findings highlight the intrinsic compromise in mucosal immune response and have important implications for the development of strategies to combat avian and zoonotic pathogens in poultry.
evidence: Inferred from the practical implications of the experimental findings.
